Your role: a new security analyst on the night shift

It’s 10:00 p.m. on a Monday at Meridian Valley Health, a hospital system in Columbus, Ohio. You’re Dana Cole. Until last month, you provided IT support for two of the hospital’s clinics. Now you’re in your first week as a security analyst, and your main tool is a screen called the alert queue.

  • About 75 to 90 minutes
  • Eight short lessons
  • Saves as you go

What alert triage is

Security tools record what happens on a network: every sign-in, every download, every change to a setting. When something looks unusual, the tool raises an alert, a message that says “this looks different from normal.”

Unusual things happen all the time for ordinary reasons. People travel, buy new laptops and work late. So a security team can receive hundreds or thousands of alerts in a single day.

Alert triage is the first review of each alert. For every alert, you decide one of three things: it needs action now, it needs a closer look, or it can be closed. The word comes from medicine: it’s French for “sorting,” and it describes how medical staff decide which patients to treat first.

Remember

Triage decides where the security team spends its time. If triage misses an attack, nobody else gets the chance to look at it.

What you’ll be able to do by the end of the shift

  1. Decide whether a sign-in alert is probably harmless or probably an attack.
  2. Find the evidence for your decision in raw logs, including what you ruled out.
  3. Check an AI assistant’s summary before you rely on it.
  4. Explain the risk to someone who isn’t technical.

Your route tonight

Each colored line is a skill you build. The cybersecurity line is the technical skill, Alert triage. The other four are durable skills you can use in any role: Thinking and Judgment, Working with AI, People and Influence, and Adaptability and Learning.

    Decide what to do with four versions of one sign-in

    Why this matters

    This is the real decision a security analyst makes dozens of times a night. Getting the feel for it now — on safe practice cards — is what lets you trust your judgment on the live alert later in the shift.

    Marcus Hart, the senior analyst on your shift, gives you four versions of the same employee’s sign-in. The first is an ordinary sign-in, for comparison. In the other three, some details change, and the changes set off an alert. For each version, you decide what to do, and then you see what Marcus decided.

    To find out what makes a sign-in alert worth acting on, decide what you would do with each version.

    1. Review the details in the card.
    2. Choose close it, look closer, or escalate.
    3. Review Marcus’s decision below the card.

    Requirement: make a decision on all four cards.

    How an expert checks a suspicious sign-in

    Marcus has worked in this security operations center for six years. Last Saturday, he checked a sign-in alert on the account of Elena Ford, a nurse manager. It isn’t tonight’s case, but the five steps he used are the same steps you’ll use tonight.

    To learn the five steps of checking a sign-in alert, review how Marcus handled one alert.

    1. Review the video one scene at a time.
    2. Pay attention to the order of Marcus’s five steps.
    3. Open the transcript if you prefer to read.

    Two terms: impossible travel and false positive

    Marcus’s video used two terms that you’ll see on every shift. Here’s what each one means.

    Impossible travel

    Picture one library card that is scanned in Columbus at 8:55 in the morning and again in Chicago at 9:10. Nobody can travel 300 miles in 15 minutes. So either two people are using the same card, or one of the scanners recorded the wrong place.

    Security tools check accounts in the same way. Impossible travel means two sign-ins to one account from places that are too far apart to reach in the time between them.

    Remember

    Impossible travel can mean someone else has the password. It can also mean the location record is wrong. Treat it as a reason to look closer, not as proof of an attack.

    False positive

    When you burn toast and the smoke alarm goes off, the alarm hasn’t failed. It did what it was built to do: it detected smoke. There just wasn’t a fire.

    A false positive is the security version of that: an alert that fires on activity that turns out to be harmless. The opposite is a true positive, an alert that catches a real problem.

    Remember

    Most alerts you review will be false positives. Your job is to tell them apart from real problems, and to record the reason for each decision.

    Tip

    Elena’s Chicago alert in Marcus’s video was a false positive. The alarm went off, but nothing was wrong.

    Why location data can be wrong

    Before you review this video

    A common assumption: the location shown on a sign-in is where the person is. Pay attention to what the video says about that assumption.

    How this applies to Marcus’s alert

    Elena’s Chicago sign-in is an example of what this video describes. Her phone was on a mobile network, and the network reported a city far from where she was. The location was wrong; Elena wasn’t. That’s why Marcus looked for a harmless explanation before he trusted the location.

    Real-world case

    A break-in where the location looked normal

    In January 2024, Microsoft disclosed that a state-backed group it calls Midnight Blizzard had broken into its corporate systems. Here’s what happened, in order.

    1. The attackers found an old test account that didn’t have multifactor authentication (a second check, such as a code on a phone) turned on.
    2. They used a password spray: they tried a few common passwords across many accounts, slowly, so that no single account recorded enough failed attempts to lock it.
    3. They sent those attempts through residential proxies, which are other people’s home internet connections. Their sign-ins looked like ordinary people signing in from home.
    4. Once inside, they took over an old test app that had wide access to Microsoft’s corporate systems. Through it, they reached email accounts, including some belonging to Microsoft’s senior leaders.

    Your decision: if you had reviewed these sign-ins, which detail would have looked normal?

    Which detail would have looked normal

    Sources: Microsoft Security Response Center, January 2024; Microsoft Threat Intelligence, “Midnight Blizzard: Guidance for responders on nation-state attack”; Infosecurity Magazine, “Microsoft Provides Defense Guidance After Nation-State Compromise”; TechTarget, “Microsoft: Legacy account hacked by Russian APT had no MFA”.

    What it means to escalate an alert

    As a first-level analyst, you’re the first person to review an alert. But you don’t have the authority to lock someone’s account or block an internet address. Those actions can stop a nurse from opening patient records or stop a billing team from working, so they belong to someone more senior.

    When you escalate an alert, you hand it to that person, the incident lead, together with your evidence and your recommendation. It works like a junior doctor calling in a senior doctor: you aren’t passing the problem on; you’re bringing in the person who can act, with everything they need.

    Warning

    If you escalate too early, you call in the incident lead for a false positive. If you escalate too late, the damage is done before anyone can act.

    Tonight, escalating means contacting Maya Stone, the incident lead on call.

    In the next four steps, you’ll gather the evidence, check the AI assistant’s summary, and decide what to do.

    Deadline: Maya expects your decision by 2:45 a.m.

    Gather evidence from each source

    To build a case you can explain to the incident lead, review every source and label the lines that matter.

    1. Review each line in the source on screen.
    2. For a line that matters, choose what it does.
    3. Choose exactly what that line shows.
    4. Go to the next source.

    Requirements: open all six sources, and label at least two lines.

    Technical stuff What each source records
    • Sign-in log: every time someone signs in to an account, with the time, the location the network reports, the device and the result.
    • MFA log: every multifactor authentication prompt, the second check sent to a phone after the password, and whether the person approved it.
    • File activity: which files an account opens, copies or downloads, and how much data moves.
    • Travel and leave records: trips and time off the employee has registered with the organization.
    • VPN settings: where the company’s VPN (virtual private network) connects to the internet. Sign-ins through the VPN show the VPN’s location, not the person’s.
    • Help desk tickets: problems the employee has reported, such as a lost phone, a locked account or a replacement laptop.

    Check the AI assistant’s summary

    The security team uses an AI assistant that writes a summary for every alert. The summary is quick to read, but it can contain mistakes. Check each claim against the evidence before you rely on it.

    To decide whether you can rely on the summary, check each claim against the evidence.

    1. Review a claim in the summary.
    2. Open the evidence reference and find the matching log line.
    3. Choose supported, contradicted, or not shown in the logs.

    Requirement: check all five claims.

          Resources

          Key terms

          Alert
          A message from a security tool that says “this looks different from normal.”
          Alert triage
          The first review of each alert: it needs action now, it needs a closer look, or it can be closed.
          False positive
          An alert that fires on activity that turns out to be harmless. A true positive catches a real problem.
          False negative
          Something is wrong and no alert fires, or someone closes a real alert too quickly.
          Impossible travel
          Two sign-ins to one account from places too far apart to reach in the time between them.
          MFA (multifactor authentication)
          A second check, such as a prompt on a phone, after the password.
          VPN (virtual private network)
          Sends a worker’s traffic through the company’s network, so sign-ins show the VPN’s location, not the person’s.
          Escalate
          Hand an alert to the person who can act, with your evidence and your recommendation.
          Corroborate
          Confirm something with more than one independent piece of evidence.
